lang.explanation: "Lang" means "long". To say something is far away, use the form "langt": "Det er langt væk" (It is far away).

langfredag.explanation: "Langfredag" means "Good Friday". It is a day off in Denmark. The name literally means "long Friday".

langs.explanation: "Langs" means "along". To say you walk next to a shore, put it before the place: "Vi går langs stranden" (We walk along the beach). To say the same with the word last, put it after the place: "Vi går stranden langs" (We walk along the beach).

langsom.explanation: "Langsom" means "slow". To say that something happens slowly, use "langsomt" (slowly): "Tal langsomt, tak" (Speak slowly, please).

langt fra.explanation: "Langt fra" means "far from". To say where something is, say the place right after it: "Hun bor langt fra byen" (She lives far from the town). To say something is far away without naming a place, use "langt væk" (far away): "Hotellet er langt væk" (The hotel is far away). To answer that something is not true at all, say "Langt fra!": "Er du sulten?" "Langt fra!" (Are you hungry? Far from it!)

langt væk.explanation: "Langt væk" means "far away". To say something is far away, end the phrase with it: "Hotellet er langt væk" (The hotel is far away). To say far from a named place, use "langt fra" (far from) with the place after it: "Hun bor langt fra byen" (She lives far from the town).

langtrukken.explanation: "Langtrukken" means "long-winded". To say a meeting takes too long, use the form ending in "-ent": "Mødet var langtrukkent" (The meeting was long-winded).

langvarig.explanation: "Langvarig" means "long-lasting". It is about how long something lasts. To say rain keeps on for a long time, say: "Der var langvarigt regn" (There was long-lasting rain). To say rain is heavy, use "kraftig" (heavy): "Der var kraftigt regn" (There was heavy rain).

larm.explanation: "Larm" means "noise". It is the noun for the verb "at larme" (to make a racket). To tell someone to stop the noise, say: "Hold op med larmen!" (Stop the noise!)

larmende.explanation: "Larmende" means "noisy". It is made from the verb "at larme" (to make a racket) plus the ending "-ende", which is like English "-ing".

latin.explanation: "Latin" means "Latin". To ask the Latin word for something, use "på" (in): "Hvad hedder det på latin?" (What is it called in Latin?). To describe a word as Latin, use "latinsk" (Latin): "et latinsk ord" (a Latin word).

latterlig.explanation: "Latterlig" means "ridiculous". It comes from "en latter" (laughter). To say someone makes a fool of themselves, use "at gøre sig latterlig" (to make oneself ridiculous): "Du gør dig latterlig" (You are making a fool of yourself).

lav.explanation: "Lav" means "low". To say prices are low, use the plural: "Priserne er lave" (The prices are low). The same spelling is also the command form of "at lave" (to make): "Lav en kop te" (Make a cup of tea).

lava.explanation: "En lava" means "lava". Do not mix it up with "lav" (low), which has no "a" at the end: "Stolen er lav" (The chair is low).

ledig.explanation: "Ledig" means "vacant". To say a job is open, use "en ledig stilling" (a job opening): "Der er en ledig stilling i butikken" (There is a job opening in the shop). To say a person has no job, use it about the person: "Han er ledig" (He is out of work).

legetøj.explanation: "Legetøj" means "toys". This word has no article, so leave out "et": "Jeg har legetøj" (I have toys). When you talk about one specific kind of toy, use its name: "en bamse" (a teddy bear).

leggings.explanation: "Leggings" means "leggings". The word comes from English and is spelled the same way. To say you are putting them on, use "tage på" (to put on): "Jeg tager leggings på" (I put on leggings).

lejlighedsvis.explanation: "Lejlighedsvis" means "occasionally". It is built from "en lejlighed" (an occasion). To say how often you play, put it after the verb: "Jeg spiller lejlighedsvis fodbold" (I play soccer occasionally).

lektier.explanation: "Lektier" means "homework". To say you do your homework, use "at lave" (to do): "Jeg laver lektier" (I do my homework). To ask a pupil whether homework is due, say: "Har du lektier for?" (Do you have homework?)

ler.explanation: "Ler" means "clay". To say what children play with, say: "Børnene leger med ler" (The children play with clay). Do not mix it up with "ler" in "Han ler" (He laughs), which is a form of "at le" (to laugh).

lesbisk.explanation: "Lesbisk" means "lesbian". It comes from the name of the Greek island Lesbos.

let.explanation: "Let" means "easy". To say a bag does not weigh much, use it for "light in weight": "en let taske" (a light bag).

letmælk.explanation: "Letmælk" means "low-fat milk". In Denmark, "letmælk" has 1.5% fat. It is built from "let" (light) and "mælk" (milk).

lettelse.explanation: "Lettelse" means "relief". To say something is a relief, say: "Det er en lettelse" (That is a relief). To say you feel relieved, use "lettet" (relieved): "Jeg er lettet" (I am relieved).

lettere.explanation: "Lettere" means "easier". It comes from "let" (easy, light). To compare weight, it also means "lighter": "en lettere taske" (a lighter bag).
